The man who offends. against the law is liable to a fine, and his plant may be seized, subject to the payment of that fine, but I do not think that his actual living and that of his family should be destroyed because he has made himself amenable to the law. That is pursuing a man to a degree that the conditions do not demand; it is not necessary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want this section to stand?

I would urge strongly that it should stand, with the view of considering the suggestion I have made.
Section stands.
On section 11-Penalty for offences by officers.

The minimum penalty here seems very high. I will certainly admit that the officer who commits a breach of his duty should be subject to serious penalty. He is in a different position altogether from a private citizen. I would not raise any objection to it, but I desire to call attention to the fact that the minimum penalty is $100.	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Unless the penalty were made very severe, there might be a temptation to infractions of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: These men are officers of the Government.
I am willing, in the charity of my heart-, not to punish even officers of this Government too severely.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-Refusing information or giving false information.

Is this penalty not very severe? Every citizen is subject to inquisitorial proceedings under this section. That might 'be all right in the case of an infraction of a very serious law, such as the law against murder or robbery, but it seems to me in the case of the enforcement of the Game Act, it is certainly a very extreme penalty.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think that the words " furnish information " might be stricken out, but we should retain the provision in regard to " wilfully furnishing false information.'/
I quite agree to that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I move that we strike out the words " wilfully refusing to furnish, or."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 16-Justice may convict on view.
This again brings in the game officer, giving him the power of a justice. I would like the minister (Mr. Roche) to reconsider that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Section stands.
On section 17-Separate offences.
What is the idea of constituting the possession of a separate part of any animal a separate offence?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It might be considered profitable for a man to kill a large number of animals, if the killing of each animal did not constitute a separate offence. He might figure on making -several thousand dollars, if the penalty were the same as if one animal had been killed.
I am referring to the words " or .separate part thereof." If a deer were killed and cut into quarters each man having a quarter would be guilty of an offence.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A person might have in his possession a portion of an animal, without having the whole animal. The possession of a separate part would constitute an offence.
If one man had a leg he would be guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He might have eaten a qfrarter of the animal.

Supposing a deer were brought into the camp and divided up amongst the friends of the man who killed it, every one of them would toe subject to the full penalty, yet none of them would be in any sense guilty. That very frequently happens.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This provision applies only where an infraction of the law has been committed and a separate part of an animal has been found in a man's possession.
I do not think it would apply to a case where a man who has committed no offence innocently becomes possessed of a portion of an animal.

A lack of 'knowledge of a breach of the law would not excuse a man,

under the wording of the Act. I appreciate the difficulty of meeting the case, but I am anxious not to make the law so drastic that there will be a combination against its enforcement. That is what is liable to take place when a law is made too comprehensive or too severe. Will the minister consider that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The executive have gone over this section several times and have drafted it as carefully as possible. However, I will allow it to stand.

The difficulty is that the gentlemen who have been advising the minister are, perhaps, not familiar with the actual conditions on the ground.
Section stands.
On section 19-Penalties.

Is it necessary or desirable to make the minimum penalty as great as it is? Indeed, is it necessary to fix any minimum penalty at all? Section 12 provides:
Any person who assaults, obstructs or Interferes with any game officer, game warden, constable or other peace officer in the discharge of any duty under the provisions of this Act or of any regulation, shall be guilty of a violation of this Act.
Section 19 applies to all cases for which no other penalty is provided. Under subsection (a), if in the excitement of the moment, a man committed a very slight offence in the way of resisting an officer, a penalty of not less than $100 would be inflicted. I should think that the minimum penalty might very well be left to the discretion of the justice of the peace in such cases. I am sure that in many cases the game officer or justice of the peace would feel that a small penalty of from $5 to $20 would amply meet the case.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Subsection (a) refers to
offences respecting wild mammals in sanctuaries or in regard to which there is no open season. It is felt that a more severe penalty should he enacted in such instances. Paragraph (d) is as follows:
A fine not exceeding one hundred dollars or less than ten dollars or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two months or to both fine and imprisonment for any other offence against this Act or any regulation.
It is not desirable to leave too much latitude to justices of the peace in inflicting these penalties. If they have the statute to guide them, they are less liable to err than if the matter is left to their own discretion.

In cases which are clearly not wilful violations of the statute, a
ten dollar or twenty dollar penalty might amply cover the offence. In such cases the magistrate has no discretion, though he is given discretion as between the $100 and $500, the minimum and maximum fines. I rather think that the minimum amount should be left out altogether.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
iSome of ,these animals
are near the point of extermination, and unless a severe penalty is provided, still further destruction will take place. I think that as a deterrent it is better to provide a minimum fine of $100 than to leave the matter to the discretion of the game officer or justice of the peace.

I think, with the member for Edmonton, that if you make the penalty too severe you really prevent the carrying out of the law, because you tend to bring about a combination of, people in the locality to prevent the enforcement of the law. Many a man might be absolutely ruined by the inflicting of so large a penalty; whereas if the matter were left to the game warden or to the magistrate, very much better results would be accomplished.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In several of the provinces the minimum penalties are in excess of the amount provided for under this Act. In Alberta there is a maximum penalty of $500 and a minimum of $200 for killing certain animals. In British Columbia there is a minimum penalty of $250 and a maximum penalty of $500 for killing big game, big game being defined in the Act as including mountain sheep, mountain goat, elk, deer, bear, etc. In Saskatchewan, there is a maximum penalty of $300 for certain offences with regard to beaver. There is no minimum.
That is wise.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Manitoba Game Act
provides penalties of from $100 to $500. In Nova Scotia the penalties are from not less than $50 to $200. In nearly all the provinces the minimum penalties are higher than the minimum penalty stated in this Act.

The minimum penalties
in the provinces are applicable to oases where men go out from civilization, generally with malice aforethought, to kill. In the Northwest Territories, that is entirely the exceptional condition. We are dealing, in the Northwest Territories, with a population, such as it is, that is dependent on the hunt for its actual living, whereas all the game laws of the provinces

were made, not in regard to people who are dependent on the game for their food and support, but to control the actions of people who hunt for sport, for amusement or for the market. Therefore, the justification for a heavy minimum fine in the provinces is on a different footing altogether from the justification for a heavy minimum fine in the Northwest Territories- Money is very scarce in the Northwest Territories, and $100 is just as far beyond the possibility of being raised by many of those who might be arrested, as $1,000 might be beyond the possibility of a hunter in the provinces my hon. friend has mentioned. I urge, in fairness and in the interest of the successful enforcement of the law, that if there is to be a minimum fine, it be reduced very substantially from the figure suggested.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
So far as the natives in
the Territories are concerned, they are exempted from many of the provisions of this Act in order to afford them an opportunity to secure a sufficient food supply, unless they violate the law in some sanctuary. This legislation is designed to hit those who are coming in for exploiting purposes, and organized bands of hunters to go into the Northwest' Territories. One of the reasons for bringing in this legislation is that we have information of Americans going in through the North Passage and coming down and establishing trading posts in various parts of the country. I do not think the penalty is too severe for the class to which I refer, and that is the class to which this legislation will principally apply.

If applied to that class
of people, then the conditions are just the same as in the various provinces, and the minimum penalty is all right. There would be no difficulty, however, in securing the application of a maximum penalty to those outside hunters who are hunting for sport or for the market, and a smaller minimum penalty then would not cause the local people to enter into combination for the purpose of setting the law at defiance which is what in human nature, they will be inclined to do if they are up against so severe a penalty as this. This means ruin to many of those people who have very little to come and go on-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The minimum penalty to which the hon. gentleman refers, more particularly concerns those valuable animals like the musk-ox which are pretty nearly extinct and whose destruction is a 
very serious matter, and it also refers to sanctuaries; but if my hon. friend looks at the other clauses he will see that in clause (b) the fine is "not exceeding $200 or less than $25''; in clause (c) the fine is "not exceeding $200 or less than $50"; and in clause (d) the fine is "not exceeding $100 or less than $10".

If the minister should see fit to state in a revised section 4 just what animals he is going to protect permanently, then this subsection might very well be quite in order. I would not at all object to a minimum penalty of $100 for the killing of a musk-ox or a buffalo. That penalty is likely as small as it should be; but not knowing from this measure what animals are going to be under protection, I naturally felt anxious about the imposition of such a heavy minimum penalty. Clause (b) imposes a minimum penalty of $25 or imprisonment of two months for any person who offends against a regulation regarding birds. That minimum is surely extremely high. The necessities of life at times demand that a wild fowl be taken and used, and there should be a very wide discretion left to a justice of the peace in regard to the penalty to be inflicted for an offence against a regulation relating to wild birds.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The preceding section refers to birds nearly extinct and in sanctuaries, that is, the more valuable birds, and the fine will be imposed only in such cases.

It would be better if we had the particulars as to what birds were going to be permanently protected and what sanctuaries were likely to be created. Is it a policy of the Government to create any sanctuaries in the Northwest Territory?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That has not been definitely decided, although it has been under consideration.
Would there be sanctuary merely for a particular kind of game or for all game?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When a sanctuary is
created, it includes all game within that area.

This clause is not limited to birds in sanctuaries; it refers to birds in regard to which there is no open season. Take for instance prairie chicken. Suppose there was a regulation passed making a close season for two or three years for prairie chicken. A person shooting a prairie chicken during that period, although he may require it for his sustenance as he may be

on the point of starvation, is brought before a magistrate and must be fined an amount not less than $25. That is a very extreme fine, and my experience in regard to fishery regulations is that extreme penalties prevent the laws from being carried out, they prevent punishment; whereas if you have reasonable penalties and reasonable administration of the laws, very much better results would be secured.
Does the hon. gentleman also want this section to stand?

My hon. friend from
Edmonton is particularly urging that it stand.

I would ask the minister to take into consideration the remarks of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in which I strongly concur, and I would also draw his attention to subsection (e) which provides for the confiscation of property.
I take the strongest possible exception to that provision which imposes a terrible and unnecessary hardship. If a man pays his fine, he should not have his property confiscated.

I also want to add my protest against that. If a man is arrested and fined it should not be obligatory to confiscate his property. In aggravated cases that might be justified, but here it is made obligatory on the game warden actually to confiscate the property of every man who is found guilty of an offence. Take the case of a man who shoots a prairie chicken, which he might actually need for food; he will be fined not less than $25, and the gun which he had used on that occasion would be confiscated. I think the punishment is entirely too severe.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
All these criticisms tend rather to the protection of the persons, as the hon. member says, rather than to the protection of the game. Now we are trying to have our legislation do both; we desire to protect our game for the future welfare of our people, and unless we have penalties that will act as a deterrent I am afraid there will be many infractions of the law.
. I think that if exploiters go into that country and break the law-the natives themselves are exempt-they should be subject to a very severe penalty. In many cases the animals these exploiters kill are the most valuable ones, or of species which are rapidly nearing the point of extinction. I think the case cited by the hon. member about the prairie chicken would come under another provision of the Act, where
not such a severe penalty is imposed. However, I am willing to allow the section to stand for further consideration, if hon. gentlemen consider the penalties too severe.

I infer from the attitude of my hon. friend from Edmonton that he is sincerely desirous of seeing the game protected; so am I. But I do not think you will have the same satisfactory enforcement of the law where you have these extreme penalties. The game warden will perhaps be living in the same community with the man who commits an offence, and might reason: "The moment I convict him I have to deprive him of his means of livelihood; rather than do that I will let him go scot free." That is the way in which, our fishery laws are administered, or non-administered. In many cases the penalties are so severe that there is a feeling of sympathy among the officers, and rather than ruin the man guilty of an offence they will close their eyes to an infraction of the law. There is no benefit in having a law on the statute book that is not enforced, although many people think that once a law is on the statute book it is all right even if it is not enforced. I do not believe that; I think it is better to have a law that can be enforced in a reasonable way.
Section stands.
On section 22-commencement of Act:
What is the object in bringing the Act into force by proclamation instead of in the ordinary way?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: By one of these clauses certain regulations are to be enacted, and we do not wish to have the Act come into force until these regulations are formulated.

The regulations will
come into force at the same time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir George Foster, the House adjourned at 6 p.m.
Monday, July 23, 1917.
